lead: A compression-ignition (CI) engine compresses only air, to about 17 : 1, so the air near TDC (about 800 to 900 K) is far above the temperature at which diesel fuel ignites by itself. Fuel is sprayed in near the end of compression and has to break up, evaporate and mix before it can burn. So the charge is never uniform, mixing and burning overlap, and combustion runs in four stages: ignition delay, premixed burning, mixing-controlled burning and late burning. The ignition delay decides how much fuel collects before burning starts, and that decides how hard the engine runs.
prereq: You need: fuel injection, nozzles and spray formation (fuel injection systems), and crank-angle timing (stages of combustion).

sections.h3: Nature of the charge and mixture formation

blocks.text: The CI charge is heterogeneous: at any instant the cylinder holds liquid droplets, fuel vapour, rich zones, lean zones and plain air. The overall air–fuel ratio is always lean (from about 18 : 1 at full load to over 80 : 1 at idle), because load is controlled by the amount of fuel, not by throttling the air. Yet burning happens only where the local mixture is near stoichiometric.

Mixture formation happens in three steps. The jet leaving the nozzle at high pressure breaks up into droplets (atomisation); the droplets take heat from the hot air and evaporate (vaporisation); and air motion and the spray's own momentum carry air into the vapour (mixing). Swirl and squish help the last step (see air motion).
Plot the heat release rate, dQ/dθ in joules per degree, against crank angle. It shows the stages more clearly than the pressure trace.

items: Ignition delay (A to B): from the start of injection to the start of combustion. Nothing burns yet, but fuel keeps entering, breaking up and mixing. The delay has a physical part (atomisation, vaporisation, mixing) and a chemical part (pre-flame reactions that build up radicals). It ends where the pressure trace first rises above the motoring curve, or where the heat release rate first turns positive.

Premixed (rapid) combustion (B to C): the fuel that mixed during the delay ignites at many points almost at once and burns very fast. The heat release rate shows a sharp spike and the pressure rises steeply. A long delay means more fuel in this stage and a harder, noisier spike.

Mixing-controlled combustion (C to D): the rest of the fuel burns as fast as it can mix with air, in a diffusion flame round each spray plume. The rate is set by mixing, not chemistry, so it can be controlled by the injection rate. Most of the heat is released here, at a gentler slope.

Late combustion (after D): after injection ends, the last fuel, soot and CO burn slowly in the expansion stroke as mixing finds them. Too long a late stage wastes heat and raises smoke and exhaust temperature.

blocks.text: Some books call the first three stages the delay period, the period of rapid combustion and the period of controlled combustion; the ideas are the same. A clean CI pressure trace peaks a few degrees after TDC.

Why
rows: hotter air and walls speed both parts of the delay
denser air, faster heat transfer and reactions
the fuel ignites more easily (shorter chemical delay)
more turbulence and less heat loss, but each ms covers more degrees

blocks.text: Injection timing has an optimum. Air temperature peaks at TDC, so injecting about 10° to 15° bTDC gives the shortest delay. Injecting much earlier puts fuel into cooler air, and injecting after TDC puts it into air that is already expanding and cooling; both lengthen the delay. A cold start is the worst case: cold air, cold walls and low cranking speed give a long delay, a big premixed spike and the familiar clatter.

examples.question: A CI engine (bore 100 mm, stroke 110 mm, compression ratio 17) runs at 2000 rev/min. Injection starts at 15° bTDC and delivers 40 mg of fuel at a steady rate over 25° of crank angle. The ignition delay is 0.9 ms. (a) Find the delay in degrees and the angle at which combustion starts. (b) When does injection end? (c) How much fuel, and what share of the charge, has been injected before ignition? (d) At 2500 rev/min the delay falls to 0.8 ms. Find it in degrees and the start of combustion for the same injection timing.
steps: Start of combustion: −15° + 10.8° = −4.2°, that is 4.2° bTDC (point B).
End of injection: −15° + 25° = +10°, that is 10° aTDC.
Injection rate: 40 mg ÷ 25° = 1.6 mg/°. Fuel injected during the delay: 1.6 × 10.8 = 17.3 mg.
Share: 17.3 ÷ 40 = 0.43, so 43 % of the fuel is in the cylinder before anything burns.
At 2500 rev/min: 0.006 × 2500 = 15 °/ms, so 0.8 ms is 12.0°. Combustion starts at −15° + 12° = −3°, that is 3° bTDC.
examples.answer: (a) 10.8°, combustion starts at 4.2° bTDC. (b) Injection ends at 10° aTDC. (c) 17.3 mg, 43 % of the fuel. (d) 12.0°, start at 3° bTDC: the delay is shorter in time but longer in degrees, so injection is advanced at higher speed.

traps: The CI delay is measured from the start of injection, not from TDC or from any spark; a CI engine has no spark.
Speed shortens the delay in milliseconds but lengthens it in crank degrees. Say which unit you mean.
Injection timing has an optimum near 10° to 15° bTDC: "retarding always shortens the delay" is wrong once injection moves past TDC.
A long delay enlarges the premixed stage, not the mixing-controlled one.
Cetane number is for diesel ignition quality; octane number is for petrol knock resistance. A high-cetane fuel has a low octane number.

quiz.q: Define the ignition delay of a CI engine, in both units.
quiz.a: The interval from the start of injection to the start of combustion, given as a time (ms) or as crank angle (°CA).

quiz.q: Name the two parts of the delay period.
quiz.a: The physical delay (atomisation, vaporisation and mixing) and the chemical delay (pre-flame reactions).

quiz.q: Why does a CI engine run at an overall lean air–fuel ratio yet burn near stoichiometric?
quiz.a: Load is set by the fuel quantity and the air is not throttled, so the cylinder has excess air overall; but the flame lives only in the zones round each spray where the local mixture is near stoichiometric.

quiz.q: Why is the heat release rate in the mixing-controlled stage gentler than in the premixed stage?
quiz.a: It is limited by how fast fuel and air mix, which follows the injection rate; the premixed stage burns fuel that had already mixed during the delay, all at once.

quiz.q: Injection starts at 10° bTDC and the delay is 12°CA. Find the start of combustion.
At 1500 rev/min the delay is 1.5 ms. Find it in degrees.
A cold engine at cranking speed (200 rev/min) has a delay of 4 ms. Find the delay in degrees and explain the noisy start.
quiz.a: 0.006 × 200 × 4 = 4.8°. Few degrees, but 4 ms is a long time: cold air and walls make the delay long, a large share of the fuel collects, and the premixed spike is violent.

quiz.q: How do a higher injection pressure and a later injection each change the delay?
quiz.a: Higher pressure gives finer droplets, so the physical delay and the premixed spike shrink. Later injection shortens the delay while it moves towards TDC, but lengthens it again past TDC and pushes the burn into expansion, raising exhaust temperature and smoke.

beyond: Common-rail engines split each injection into pilot, main and post injections to shape the heat release curve; the pilot burns first and shortens the main delay. Engineers compute the heat release curve from measured pressure and fit delay correlations of the Arrhenius type. Search for diesel heat release analysis, ignition delay correlation and pilot injection.

figure.caption: Heat release rate of the worked example’s diesel at 2000 rev/min: injection starts at A (15° bTDC), nothing burns during the 10.8° delay while 17.3 mg collects, that fuel feeds the premixed spike from B (4.2° bTDC), and the rest burns as it mixes.

spec.aria: Heat release rate against crank angle. Injection runs from 15 degrees before to 10 degrees after TDC. Shaded bands mark the delay up to 4.2 degrees before TDC, a premixed spike peaking near 128 joules per degree at TDC, a mixing-controlled hump near 44 joules per degree around 12 degrees after TDC, and a late burning tail to 60 degrees.
